title: Website Redesign SEO for Estate Planning Firms: Keep Your Rankings
meta: How an estate planning firm can redesign its website without losing Google rankings: what to check before, during and after launch, and what to ask your agency.
h1: Website Redesign SEO: How Estate Planning Firms Can Redesign Without Losing Rankings
lead: A new website is exciting. The old one looks dated, the photos are from a different decade and the trust pages read like they were written for a printed brochure. So the firm hires a designer, picks a fresh look and launches. A few weeks later the calls about wills and trusts slow down. Pages that used to rank for living trust lawyer in your town have vanished, and nobody can say why. This happens to estate planning firms all the time, and it is almost always avoidable. A redesign does not have to cost you rankings. It just has to be planned with SEO in mind from the first meeting. This guide explains how website redesign SEO works, what to check before, during and after launch, and how to work with your designer and SEO agency so the new site ranks better than the old one.
quick_answer: Website redesign SEO is the work of protecting and improving your search rankings when you rebuild your website. For an estate planning firm, it means recording which pages bring in traffic and enquiries today, keeping or improving the content that ranks, mapping every old URL to its new home with permanent redirects, carrying over titles, headings and structured data, checking speed and mobile use before launch, and watching Search Console closely for several weeks afterward. Bring your SEO agency in before design starts, not after launch, because most ranking losses come from decisions made early, such as dropping pages, changing URLs or cutting content.
takeaways: Bring your agency in before the design starts, not after launch.
Record your top pages, searches and enquiries before changing anything.
Each old page needs a clear new home and a permanent redirect.
Do not cut the content that brings in trust and probate enquiries.
Check speed, mobile use, forms and tracking on the new site.
Monitor Search Console and enquiries closely for several weeks.

sections.answer: It is the SEO planning and checking that protects your rankings and enquiries when you rebuild or restyle your website.
paras: Most redesigns focus on how the site looks and feels: new colors, new photos, a cleaner layout and easier navigation. Those matter. But Google does not rank a site because it is pretty. It ranks pages because of their content, their structure, their links and how well they serve the searcher. A redesign can change all of those, often without anyone meaning to.

Website redesign SEO is the work of making sure the new site keeps everything that helped the old one rank, and improves on it where it can. It covers which pages exist, what their addresses are, what they say, how they link together, how fast they load and how they are tracked. It runs alongside the design work from the start, rather than being bolted on at the end.

Google itself suggests that the best time to bring in SEO help is before a redesign, adding that the earlier, the better. That way the site can be built to be search friendly from the ground up, instead of being patched after the rankings have already slipped.

sections.h2: Why Do Estate Planning Firms Lose Rankings After a Redesign?
sections.answer: Usually because pages were removed, URLs changed without redirects, content was cut or the new site is slower or harder for Google to read.
paras: The most common cause is changed addresses. The old site had a page at one URL for living trusts and another for probate. The new site moves them, renames them or merges them, and nobody tells Google where they went. Every link pointing to the old pages now hits an error, and the rankings those pages earned are lost.

The second cause is cut content. Designers often prefer short pages with lots of white space. But many estate planning searches are research searches. People want to understand the difference between a will and a trust, what probate involves in their state or how to plan for a parent with dementia. If the long, helpful pages that answered those questions are trimmed to a few lines, they stop ranking.

Other causes are technical. A new site might load slowly on phones, hide text inside images or scripts that Google struggles to read, drop the page titles and descriptions that were written for search, or accidentally block search engines entirely. Each of these can be avoided with a little planning.

sections.h2: When Should You Involve Your SEO Agency?
sections.answer: Before the designer starts, so SEO shapes the site plan, the page list and the URLs from day one.
paras: Many firms bring in SEO help after launch, when the traffic has already dropped. By then the fix is harder, because the decisions that caused the problem are built into the new site. Involving your agency at the planning stage is far cheaper and far more effective than repairing damage later.

At the start, your agency can tell the designer which pages bring in the most enquiries, which ones must be kept, which searches each page should target and what structure will help Google understand your practice areas. That shapes the site map, the navigation and the content plan before a single design is drawn.

If you work with a single provider for both design and SEO, the same rule applies. Ask to see the SEO plan for the redesign before design work begins, and make sure someone is responsible for protecting your rankings, not just making the site look good.

sections.h2: What Should You Record Before Changing Anything?
sections.answer: Your current top pages, the searches they rank for, their traffic and enquiries, and a full list of every URL on the site.
paras: Before anything changes, take a snapshot of how the current site performs. Use Google Search Console to list the pages that get the most clicks and the searches each one appears for. Use your analytics and call tracking to see which pages lead to calls and forms. Note your current position in the map pack for your main searches, such as estate planning attorney near me.

Then make a complete list of every page on the current site, including old blog posts, practice pages, attorney bios and any landing pages from past campaigns. A crawl tool can do this quickly. Pages you have forgotten about may still bring in traffic or have links from other sites.

This baseline does two jobs. It tells the team what must be protected, and it gives you something to compare against after launch. Without it, you cannot tell whether a change in enquiries is caused by the redesign or by something else.

sections.h2: Which Pages and Content Should You Keep?
sections.answer: Keep every page that brings traffic, links or enquiries, and keep or improve the content that makes it rank.
paras: A redesign is a good moment to tidy up, but cutting should be deliberate. Any page that ranks for useful searches, brings in enquiries or has links from other sites should be kept, merged into a stronger page or redirected to its closest match. Pages with no traffic, no links and no value to clients can be retired, but they still need a sensible redirect.

Protect the content that earns trust. Estate planning is a considered decision, often made over weeks. People read about wills, trusts, powers of attorney, guardianship and probate before they call. Pages that explain those topics clearly, in plain language, are often the ones that rank and convert. A redesign should make them easier to read, not shorter.

It is also a chance to fill gaps. If your old site had one page covering all estate planning services, the new one might have separate pages for living trusts, wills, probate, trust administration and elder law. Our guide on [[a:blog/how-to-get-estate-planning-clients|how to get estate planning clients]] explains how those pages support enquiries.

sections.h2: How Do You Map Old URLs to New Ones?
sections.answer: List every old URL, decide its new home and set up a permanent redirect for each one that changes.
paras: The single most important step in redesign SEO is URL mapping. Google's own guidance on site moves tells site owners to prepare a URL mapping from the current URLs to their corresponding new format. In practice that is a simple spreadsheet: old address in one column, new address in the next.

Every old page should point somewhere sensible. A page about revocable living trusts should point to the new living trust page, not the home page. A retired blog post should point to the most closely related page that still exists. Sending everything to the home page loses much of the value the old pages built up.

Where possible, keep URLs the same. If the old address for your probate page was clear and sensible, there is often no reason to change it. Fewer changes mean fewer redirects and less risk. Change URLs only when the new structure is genuinely better.

sections.h2: What Kind of Redirects Should You Use?
sections.answer: Permanent server-side redirects, usually 301s, from each old address straight to its new one.
paras: A redirect tells browsers and search engines that a page has moved. For a redesign, the right type is a permanent redirect, which tells Google the new address should replace the old one in search results. Google recommends a permanent server-side redirect when a page's URL changes, because it has the best chance of being understood correctly.

Each redirect should go straight from the old address to the final new address. Chains, where one redirect leads to another and then another, slow things down and can lose value along the way. If your site has been redesigned before, check for old redirects that now point to pages that are moving again, and update them to point to the final destination.

Test every redirect before launch on a staging copy of the site, and again straight after launch. Broken redirects and error pages are among the most common, and most avoidable, causes of lost rankings after a redesign.

sections.h2: What On-Page Details Must Carry Over?
sections.answer: Page titles, meta descriptions, headings, internal links, structured data and image alt text.
paras: Many of the details that help a page rank are invisible to visitors. Page titles and meta descriptions, written for search, are often lost when content moves into a new template. Headings get restyled and reworded. Structured data that told Google your firm's name, address, phone number and practice areas gets left behind. Each of these should be carried over or improved.

Internal links matter too. The old site may have linked from the wills page to the trust page and from blog posts to the relevant practice pages. Those links help Google understand which pages are most important and how topics relate. Rebuild them deliberately on the new site rather than leaving each page isolated.

Finally, check that text is real text. Some design approaches place key words inside images or load content in ways search engines find harder to read. Your agency can check that each page's main content is visible to Google before launch.

sections.h2: How Do You Make Sure the New Site Is Fast and Mobile Friendly?
sections.answer: Test speed and mobile use on the staging site before launch, using the same measures Google uses.
paras: Many estate planning clients are older, and many adult children research planning options for their parents on their phones. A site that is slow or awkward on a phone loses them. Google's Core Web Vitals measure real-world user experience for loading performance, interactivity and visual stability, and they are a sensible benchmark for any new site.

Large images, heavy video backgrounds, fancy animations and long lists of plugins are the usual culprits. They can make a site look impressive in a design review and frustrating in real life. Ask your designer and agency to test the staging site on an ordinary phone connection, not just on a fast office computer.

Accessibility belongs in the same check. Clear text, good contrast, readable font sizes and buttons that are easy to tap help every visitor, especially older ones. A site that is easy to use is more likely to turn a visit into a consultation.

sections.h2: What Should You Check on Launch Day?
sections.answer: That search engines can crawl the site, redirects work, forms and tracking fire and the sitemap is submitted.
paras: Staging sites are usually hidden from search engines, and that setting sometimes gets carried over to the live site by mistake. On launch day, confirm that the new site is open to search engines and that no pages are accidentally marked noindex. This one setting has wiped out more redesigns than any other.

Then test the essentials. Click through the main redirects. Submit each contact and consultation form and confirm the enquiry arrives. Check that call tracking numbers display correctly and that analytics records visits and enquiries. Submit the new sitemap in Google Search Console.

Update anything outside the website that points to it. Your Google Business Profile link, legal directory listings and any important links you control should point to the new addresses where they have changed. Small details like these help Google settle on the new site faster.

sections.h2: What Should You Watch in the Weeks After Launch?
sections.answer: Search Console errors, indexing, clicks for your key pages, map visibility and, most of all, enquiries.
paras: Some movement in rankings after a redesign is normal while Google processes the changes. What matters is the trend over the following weeks. Your agency should check Search Console regularly for crawl errors, pages that are not being indexed and drops in clicks for the pages you recorded in your baseline.

Compare enquiries against the baseline too. If calls and forms about trusts and probate hold steady or rise, the redesign is doing its job. If they fall, the baseline shows which pages lost ground, which points straight to the likely cause, such as a missing redirect or cut content.

Plan for a short period of follow-up fixes. Even careful redesigns turn up a few broken links, missed redirects or pages that need more content. Catching and fixing these quickly is what separates a redesign that improves rankings from one that quietly loses them. Our guide on [[a:blog/seo-retainer|what an SEO retainer should include]] covers how this kind of ongoing work usually fits into a monthly plan.

sections.h2: What Should You Ask Your Designer and Agency Before You Start?
sections.answer: Who protects the rankings, how URLs will be mapped, what content will change and how success will be measured.
paras: Before work begins, ask a few direct questions. Who is responsible for protecting our rankings during the redesign? Will you record our current performance first? How will you map old URLs to new ones and test the redirects? Which pages and content are you planning to change or remove, and why?

Ask about the technical side as well. Will the new site be fast on phones? Will page titles, descriptions and structured data carry over? How will you check that search engines can crawl the site at launch? Who will monitor Search Console afterward, and for how long?

Clear answers to these questions are a good sign. Vague ones suggest that SEO has not been planned into the project. If your designer and SEO agency are different teams, put them in touch early so they agree on who does what. Our page on [[a:estate-planning-seo-company|working with an estate planning SEO company]] explains how we approach it.

faq.q: Will Redesigning My Website Hurt My SEO?
faq.a: It can, but it does not have to. Most losses come from removed pages, changed URLs without redirects, cut content or technical mistakes, all of which careful planning can avoid.

faq.q: How Do I Redesign My Website Without Losing SEO?
faq.a: Record current performance, keep content that ranks, map every old URL to a new one with permanent redirects, carry over on-page details and test everything before and after launch.

faq.q: When Should I Involve My SEO Agency in a Redesign?
faq.a: Before the design starts. Early decisions about pages, URLs and content cause most ranking losses, and they are much easier to get right at the planning stage.

faq.q: Should I Change My URLs During a Redesign?
faq.a: Only when the new structure is clearly better. Keeping sensible URLs the same reduces redirects and risk. Any URL that changes needs a permanent redirect.

faq.q: How Long Does It Take Rankings to Settle After a Redesign?
faq.a: Some movement in the first few weeks is normal. With redirects and content in place, rankings usually settle over the following weeks, though it varies by site.

faq.q: What Is the Most Common Redesign SEO Mistake?
faq.a: Missing redirects, closely followed by leaving the new site blocked from search engines after launch. Both are easy to check and easy to fix.
